doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

title: Basie's improvised intros and helping new men
summary: Basie noodled at the piano before picking tunes; players knew intros, and nobody sabotaged newcomers.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Let me ask you a question about this. Is this true they said that in between tunes, Basie would just start playing the piano and you wouldn’t always know what tune was gonna come next?

That’s right. He would just fiddle around, while he’s trying to think of a tune, he might be looking you dead in the face. And you’d think he’s looking — oh, he’s looking at me, and he’s looking abstractly, and not even thinking about what he’s looking at, but thinking about what song it’s gonna be. And most times he’d be humming. [humms] And then he’d think of something and he’d go into an intro, which we all knew what the intros were, you know. But it would be so smooth that the people would wonder, how the hell did they get to that tune?

At some point during his meanderings we would know exactly what the tune was going to be. And some of them have similar introductions. Like “Down for the Count” had the same kind of introduction as another song that was in A flat [humms]. I don’t know what it was, but there were two songs that had similar introductions, but somehow when it came time to hit letter A, you knew which song it was going to be. That was like amazing. I still can’t figure that out.

Now John Heard told us that his first night on the band Basie did that and he’s going, he’s saying “what’s the tune” and one guy told him it’s number 4 and one guy told him it’s number 11. You guys wouldn’t do that, would you? Of course but he said he couldn’t read music anyway so it didn’t matter.
Wait a minute, you’re not talking about John Heard?
I think he was putting us on.
John had a good time while he was here.

But going back to that, when they’re setting up the intros like that, and a new guy comes on the band, okay, so he maybe doesn’t know this routine. Did you guys ever, when the new guy is sitting there saying “what tune is it,” did you generally bail him out by helping him with what tune? Or did you sabotage him —

Oh, no, he didn’t even have to ask. As soon as Basie started in, as soon as it was known what tune it was, he’d say, “Corner Pocket” or whatever. The idea of sabotaging someone was taboo, because that would affect the overall sound of the band, it might displease Basie, and someone in the audience might pick it up and say “well they’re not too together, are they?” So that was, even if you didn’t like someone personally, the idea of sabotaging —

What did happen sometimes is if Basie felt like he was taking a little long getting to what we call a “joiner,” [humms] he would go into it a little fast before the guy could find the music and you’re stuck trying to play your part and tell the guy next you, if he’s new, you know, what number to get up. And in that case you’d see the guy scrambling, you know, and he’s not able to play until he gets the part up.
But it’s not a sabotage thing at all.
